newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY FIRE BOMBINGS CONTINUE AFTER FATAL BLAST.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY FIRE BOMBINGS CONTINUE AFTER FATAL BLAST.

text.p: Hungarian police said a music club and restaurant in Budapest was set ablaze by petrol bombs early on Monday, four days after a handgrenade killed two people at another restaurant.
The latest petrol bombing comes amid a spate of similar attacks in the Hungarian capital that police have blamed on a gangland war they so far have been unable to stop.

Diplomats and political analysts said the attacks, which began last September, have not touched the country's vital tourist business, but pose an increasingly significant political problem for the socialist-led government.

Police said the latest attack happened at about 5:30 a.m. when an unidentified person, possibly with accomplices, threw petrol bombs into the garden of a Greek restaurant and club on stylish Andrassy Ut. The bombs set the garden and a roof ablaze but caused no injuries.
The blaze was quickly extinguished and the Hungarian MTI news agency said firefighters prevented a major explosion by removing five gas cylinders from the area.
"The investigation is going on to determine the damage the Molotov cocktails have caused," Budapest police spokesman Endre Nagy told Reuters.
The attack comes after a handgrenade killed a Chinese restauranteur's wife and daughter when it exploded in the restaurant toilet early on Friday morning, after the premises had closed.
Police said it was too soon to say if there was any link between the latest attacks and earlier ones, which have resulted in property damage and at least one death previously.

Since last September, Budapest has been shaken by more than a dozen bombings and at least a half dozen shootings in an apparent gangland war. One known gangland figure was killed last year when he was shot dead at the wheel of his car.
Members of Budapest's Chinese community said the bombing on Friday at the Great Wall Restaurant did not bear the hallmarks of a Chinese gangland-style attack.

"I suspect the Russian mafia. They are jealous because we have many more shops in Budapest than they, only they forget that we succeed by work and not by crime," a Chinese storeowner identified only as Mr Ziang told the Blikk newspaper.
Diplomats said the attacks seemed designed to avoid harming the general public.
"It seems this is not directed against the general public," a diplomat said, adding that the police were doing all in their power to solve the case because "it affects their image".

Political analyst Tibor Vidos said the wave of violence posed an increasingly serious political problem for Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze, who sacked three police generals of the national police in a major shakeup late last year.
"In the case of a well-organised underground it is difficult for police to infiltrate," Vidos said.
"I think it's going to hurt the reputation of the minister of interior, but I don't think it's going to hurt the reputation of the country," he added.
